title: The Conker Tree
paragraphs:
I have stood in this playground
for a hundred years,
my roots gripping the earth
like an old man’s fingers.
I have watched the children grow up,
and their children,
and their children’s children.

In spring, I unfold my leaves
like a thousand green hands
and hold up my flowers,
white candles
to light the playground.

In summer, I am an umbrella of shade.
Children sit beneath my branches,
sharing sandwiches and secrets.
I keep their secrets.
I never tell.

In autumn, I drop my treasures:
glossy conkers, brown as polished shoes,
hidden in spiky green cases.
The children shriek and scramble
and stuff their pockets full,
and I feel richer than a king.

In winter, the children hurry past me,
hoods up and heads down.
The wind rattles my bare branches.
Snow settles on my shoulders
like a heavy white shawl,
and I shiver,
and I wait.

But I am patient.
I have waited through a hundred winters,
and every spring the children run back to me:
the shouts, the skipping ropes,
the football thudding against my trunk.
I have stood in this playground for a hundred years.
I will stand here for a hundred more.

questions.prompt:
Look at the first stanza.
For how long has the tree stood in the playground?

Look at the first stanza.
The tree’s roots grip the earth ‘like an old man’s fingers’.
What does this suggest about the roots? Tick **one**.
options: They are young and smooth.
They are old and knobbly, and they hold on tightly.
They are growing up towards the sky.
They are cold and wet from the rain.

questions.prompt:
Look at the second stanza.
What are the ‘white candles’? Tick **one**.
options: candles that the children put in the tree
snow lying on the branches
lights on the school building
the tree’s white flowers, standing up tall

questions.prompt:
Look at the third stanza.
‘In summer, I am an umbrella of shade.’
What does this tell you about the tree in summer?
questions.model: Its leafy branches spread out over the playground and keep the children out of the hot sun, just as an umbrella shelters you.
points: explaining that the tree’s branches or leaves spread out and give the children shade, or protect them from the sun.

questions.prompt:
Look at the third stanza.
‘I keep their secrets.
I never tell.’
What does this suggest about the tree?
questions.model: It suggests that the tree can be trusted: it is a loyal friend to the children.
points: a quality that fits, e.g. it can be trusted; it is loyal; it is a good friend to the children; it is kind.
Do not accept answers that take the words literally, e.g. “trees cannot talk”.

questions.prompt:
Look at the fourth stanza.
The conkers are ‘glossy’.
Which word is closest in meaning to **glossy**? Tick **one**.
options: sticky
shiny
heavy
rough

questions.prompt:
Look at the fourth stanza.
Find and copy **one** word that shows the children move quickly and untidily to get the conkers.

Look at the fifth stanza.
Find and copy **one** word that shows the tree felt cold.

Look at the whole poem.
Tick **one** box in each row to show whether each statement is **true** or **false**.
statements: The conkers grow in smooth, soft cases.
In winter, the children climb up into the tree.
In summer, children sit in the tree’s shade.

questions.prompt:
Compare the fourth stanza with the fifth stanza.
How is winter different from autumn for the tree? Tick **one**.
options: In autumn the tree feels lonely, but in winter it feels happy.
In both seasons, the children play under the tree.
In autumn the tree is busy and happy with the children, but in winter it is cold and lonely.
In autumn it snows, but in winter the sun shines.

questions.prompt: How is the poem organised? Tick **one**.
options: Each stanza is about a different child.
Stanzas 2 to 5 each describe a different season.
The seasons go backwards, from winter to spring.
Every stanza ends with the same line.

questions.prompt:
How does the tree feel about the children?
Explain, using evidence from the poem.
questions.model: The tree loves the children and cares about them. It keeps their secrets (‘I never tell’) and it feels ‘richer than a king’ when they collect its conkers. In winter it misses them and waits for them, and every spring they ‘run back’ to it.
points: Gives a feeling that fits, such as loves, cares about or misses the children.
Backs it up with words from the poem, such as ‘I never tell’, ‘richer than a king’ or ‘and I wait’.

questions.prompt:
Look at the last stanza.
Why do you think the tree says, ‘But I am patient’?
Explain, using evidence from the poem.
questions.model: The tree is patient because it knows that the children always come back. It has ‘waited through a hundred winters’, and ‘every spring the children run back to me’, so it does not mind waiting through the cold, lonely winter.
points: explaining that the tree knows the children will come back in spring (1 mark), e.g. ‘every spring the children run back to me’.
explaining that the tree is used to waiting because it is so old (1 mark), e.g. it has ‘waited through a hundred winters’.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of the whole poem? Tick **one**.
options: A tree is cut down to make room for a new playground.
Children plant a conker and watch it grow into a tree.
A tree describes one exciting day when the children found its conkers.
An old tree describes how it has watched over the children through the seasons for many years.
